# The World's Lies

> "Be careful that you don't let anyone rob you through his philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men"
>
> — Colossians 2:8

The flesh supplies the itch. The world supplies the reasons to scratch it.

This is the second cause, and it's much the bigger of the two. The Little Monster is a pipsqueak. The Big Monster is everything you've been told about him.

Your grandfather was told that this habit would send him blind, grow hair on his palms and land him in an asylum. That was nonsense, and it deserved to be laughed out of the room. But when the scare stories went, the truth went out with them. The pendulum swung the whole way over, and now a boy hears the opposite sermon, preached just as confidently. Here are its main points.

**"Everyone does it."** Nearly true. One pastor who has written honestly about it says so flatly: "Virtually every man and almost as many women have tried it." But a crowded trap is still a trap. Every man in it wishes he were out, as you saw two chapters ago. Since when did you take your direction from a crowd that's lost?

**"It's healthy. It's harmless. Doctors say so."** We said it in the introduction and we'll say it again: medicine says it doesn't hurt your body, and we won't quarrel. But the doctor is answering a question you never asked. You didn't ask whether it would damage your prostate. You asked why you can't stop, and why you feel like a smaller man afterwards. A writer for The Gospel Coalition made the distinction neatly: "But just because something isn't harmful physically doesn't mean it's not harmful spiritually." One coach, from the gym-and-hustle end of the internet, says the same about men in general: "They think it's normal. They think it's harmless, but it's actually not."

Let's give the other side its strongest voice. A researcher and therapist told a national radio programme: "Abstaining from masturbation is not a reasonable or, in my opinion, ethical treatment goal". Notice the word *treatment*. He is talking about what a clinic should prescribe to a patient, and on that he may well be right. This book isn't a clinic and you aren't its patient. You are a free man deciding what kind of man to be. No therapist has the authority to tell you that wanting to be rid of lust is unreasonable.

Grant the other side its numbers as well. A psychiatrist who treats porn addiction reckons that about three users in four are not compulsive at all, and he tells his audience so: "I'd say there's a 75 chance that you're fine". He means porn, and he means fine in the sense a clinic uses. I'll take his figure. This book has never said that every man who does this is a clinical addict. Its case rests on two things no clinic measures: what Jesus said about lust, and what men say the habit has cost them. Besides, you didn't pick up a book with this title because you were fine.

And watch what the experts do when the habit turns up in their own consulting rooms. There is a problem men call "death grip": years of the hand leave a man unable to finish, or to stay ready, with a real woman. A urologist with a large following, who says plainly "I don't think there is a problem with masturbation", gives those men this instruction: "the first thing you have to do is stop masturbating". So the doctors who say it's harmless still prescribe stopping when it does harm. We'll come back to this in a later chapter.

**"It's natural."** So is a great deal that you wouldn't copy. One preacher, who was bound by this for years himself, answers in nine words: "We also see in nature where pigs eat trash." That a thing occurs in nature tells you nothing about whether it's good for a man.

**"A man needs the release."** You need air, water and food. Go without those and you die. No man has ever been carried out of a tent after a week's camping because he couldn't get a minute alone.

**"It keeps you out of worse trouble."** The same writer answers this one: "Nowhere in Scripture are we told to commit one sin to avoid another." And it doesn't even work. Ask the men who quit porn, kept the habit, and found it was the back door.

## The lies about porn and about women {-}

The world has a second set of lies for the screen, and a third for real women.

**"Porn is just entertainment. Nobody gets hurt."** Somebody always does. You can't know whether the woman on the screen wanted to be there. Some of what sits on the biggest sites was made by force, and some of the people in it were children. In 2020 the biggest of them removed millions of videos in a single purge, because it had never checked who uploaded them. And when it is her own choice, she has been sold the same lie from the other side: that her worth is her body, and that men's hunger is a living. The lie that ruins the man who watches ruins the woman who is watched.

**"Everybody watches it."** Many do. Go back two chapters and ask them the two questions. Not one would choose it again, and not one wants it for his son or his daughter.

**"A real man gets as many women as he can."** That is the oldest of the lot. It makes a man's worth depend on being wanted, which is exactly what makes him easy to lead. A real man is one a woman can trust. Count how many of the men who live by the other rule you would trust with your sister.

**"It's only a bit of fun. She knew what it was."** Then why did you have to tell yourself so? Using a person is still using her when she agrees to it. Paul's rule is short: "that no one should take advantage of and wrong a brother or sister in this matter". You already knew that. It is why it never felt like fun the next morning.

## The quiet pulpit {-}

You'd expect the church to push back. Mostly it says nothing. A man can sit in a pew for thirty years and hear sermons on adultery, greed and gossip, and never hear this habit named once. Under one man's public testimony, a listener wrote what thousands were thinking: "This is a subject that is not addressed in the pulpit at all!" A boy hears jokes about it at school and silence about it in church, and he draws the obvious conclusion: either it doesn't matter, or it's so shameful that he must be the only one.

Some kind and respected Christians went further and waved it through. James Dobson, who helped a great many families, wrote: "It is my opinion that masturbation is not much of an issue with God." His motive was good. He wanted to spare teenagers from being crushed by guilt, and in that he was right, because guilt has never freed anyone. But he also wrote this: "Attempting to suppress this act is one campaign that is destined to fail—so why wage it?"

Read that sentence again. That is the Big Monster in a good suit: you can't stop, so don't bother. To be fair to Dobson, he listed warning signs as well, including crushing guilt, obsession, pornography, and carrying the habit into marriage. Count how many of those four describe you.

The lie gets passed along between friends too. A twenty-one-year-old wrote: "my Christian friend told me that the only thing wrong about masturbation is feeling guilty". His friend had it exactly backwards. The guilt was the one part of him still telling the truth.

Let's be fair to the other side here as well. The Bible never mentions masturbation by name. One pastor, asked where it comes up, answered honestly that it never does. If you were hoping for a verse that says "you shall not", there isn't one, and this book won't pretend there is. But Jesus didn't need to name the act, because he went behind it. He put the sin in the look and in the heart (Matthew 5:28), and that is where this habit lives. Ask yourself how often it has happened without lust, and you have your answer.

## The opposite lie {-}

There's publicity the other way, of course. Whole corners of the internet promise great things if you stop. You'll get a deeper voice, clear skin, a surge of testosterone and women turning round in the street. The biggest forum of them all started with a thread about a study claiming a testosterone spike after seven days. That study has since been retracted. A sociologist put it flatly: "There is no scientific evidence that supports the idea of these superpowers."

Logically, all that hype ought to get men out. It doesn't. In fact it helps to keep them in, and that's why I call it a lie as well.

It turns stopping into a feat. You go on "hard mode", you count days and you call yourself a warrior. Every bit of that language tells you that you're giving up something enormous in exchange for a prize. Then day thirty comes, the prize hasn't arrived, and back you go.

It also leaves lust on the throne. "Quit so you can get women" only changes what the appetite is fed. Even the men we quote gratefully in this book sometimes sell it that way. Take their honesty about what the habit costs, and leave the sales pitch. A man on the biggest of those forums says it best himself: "Semen Retention does not grant you godhood."

Both sermons, "it's good for you" and "quitting gives you powers", agree on one thing. They both say it's a big deal to stop. It isn't.

## The best liar of all {-}

The strangest thing is that the most persuasive voice in all this is your own.

Men in the trap aren't weak-willed. It takes real stamina to keep up a secret for twenty years. The trouble is where the strength goes. We pour it into defending the habit. Then, when we try to quit and fail, we turn it on ourselves. Failing at something is one thing. Hating yourself for it is another, and it leaks out into everything else: the gym you stop going to, the diet that lasts till Thursday, the temper your children get the sharp end of.

Nobody argues with himself about whether to give up golf. With this we argue every night, and we think that's normal.

So from now on, treat everything you've been told about this habit like a man selling timeshares. Smile and nod, and don't sign. That goes for "you need it" and for "it's who you are". It also goes for the idea of a safe version. "Only in the shower", "only without a screen" and "only at weekends" were all invented by the Little Monster. Keep asking the two questions: "Why am I doing this? Do I actually need to?"

Of course you don't.

Once you're in the trap, the lies get help from inside. Some part of you knows the Little Monster expects feeding, and it will defend his dinner against any argument. That's fear: the fear of that empty, fidgety feeling. You don't have to understand it. A dog has no idea how central heating works, but it knows precisely which patch of floor is warm.

## "Giving up" {-}

Our own passivity does the rest. We believe what we've always heard, and the people we trust most say it last and loudest.

The phrase "giving up" is the plainest example. It smuggles in the idea of a sacrifice. But there's nothing to give up. You'll be getting rid of a parasite and gaining a great deal. So we'll drop that phrase here and now. In this book you don't "give up" lust. You stop. You quit. Best of all, **YOU ESCAPE.**

What pulled you in to begin with was the sense that everybody else was doing it and you'd be missing out. You joined in, and you never did find the thing you were afraid of missing. The lie renews itself, though. Every joke in a film and every knowing laugh among friends says there must be something in it, or why would it be so universal? A free man can hear all that for years and then, one flat evening, think, "Maybe just once, to see." He's back inside before he knows it.

So be clear about who is missing out. It isn't the man who stopped. It's the man who carries on, who is handing over a lifetime of:

- Energy
- Time
- Confidence
- Peace of mind
- Self-respect
- Courage
- A clear conscience before God
- Freedom

And what does he get for it? **NOTHING.** Each time, he gets the brief illusion of returning to the calm that the free man has all day long.

## "I could stop if I wanted" {-}

Men believe they do it for pleasure or to relax, or because they've a high drive. The real reason is to quiet the Little Monster. The trap closes slowly. Most men don't know they're in it until the day they try to leave, and even then plenty won't admit it. Any pastor or youth leader who has raised the subject with a young man knows how the conversation goes:

"You know the only reason you keep doing it is that you can't stop?"

"Rubbish. I like it. If I didn't, I'd stop."

"Then stop for a month, just to show me."

"Why would I? I like it."

"Stop for a month to show yourself."

"There's no point. I told you, I like it."

He likes it so much that he won't risk finding out.

The world's lies are general. Your own are specific: this habit helps me with *this*, at *these* times. A writer on a Christian recovery blog gives the instruction for dealing with them: "Identify what lies you believe about the stressor and then diligently replace those lies with truth."

That's what we do next. We take the times you reach for it, one at a time.
